e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to “beasts,” naming the creatures considered or handled as a group in the Old Testament. It appears seven times in six verses, including passages involving travel, property responsibility, community need, and the provision of water. Its use therefore points to living creatures in ordinary communal, agricultural, or wilderness settings rather than to a person or an abstract idea.

Addan is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Bible, this name appears once, in Ezra 2:59, and is rendered “Addan.” Because it functions as a name, its meaning is primarily identification: it distinguishes one person from others in the account. The name itself does not provide enough information to explain the person’s character, ancestry, or role; those details must come from the surrounding passage and related statements.

It describes the outer limits that distinguish one territory from another, especially when land is assigned, described, or spoken of as belonging to a people. It occurs 10 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages about Israel’s territorial boundaries and the division of the nations. The surrounding verse determines whether “borders” or “coasts” best fits the immediate setting.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “carried.” It expresses the condition of being carried away, especially in passages describing people moved from their land or community. Rather than naming the act of carrying itself, it can identify those affected by that movement or describe their carried-away state. The word occurs 43 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with especially frequent use in Ezra, Ezekiel, and Jeremiah. Its surrounding context determines the precise force in each sentence.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “violent,” describing something marked by violence. It functions as a description of harmful conduct or conditions, rather than naming a person or place. In the Old Testament, it occurs two times: once in Ecclesiastes and once in Ezekiel. Its use in both passages presents violence as a serious wrong associated with injustice and death, while the surrounding verse determines the precise force of the description.

This Hebrew word means “wheel,” referring to a round object used in movement or work. It functions as a noun and appears once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 28:28. Its precise role there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word itself names the wheel rather than an action or quality. The repeated rendering “wheel” supports this basic meaning without requiring additional translation senses.

This Hebrew word is a proper name rendered “Dan.” It functions as a name rather than a general description or action word. In the Hebrew corpus represented here, it occurs twice, with both occurrences in 2 Samuel 24:6. The available lexical evidence supports this basic naming function, while the precise referent and force in that verse depend on the surrounding passage. The word is therefore best understood as identifying “Dan,” not as expressing an action or quality.

It can describe a memorial commanded by God, such as one connected with Israel’s worship, and it can also concern whether someone or something remains remembered. The word occurs 24 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a recurring emphasis on remembering rather than forgetting. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

e.t: This Hebrew word means "cry"—an audible appeal that expresses urgent distress or calls for attention. It can describe the cry of people suffering, pleading, or seeking a response. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 19 times, showing a recurring scriptural pattern in which distress is voiced rather than hidden. Its use is associated with speech and with actions or conditions that bring a cry forth. The precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word refers to a “company,” meaning people considered together as a collective body. It identifies such a company rather than describing an action or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 34:8. Because the available occurrence record does not include the verse text or surrounding context, the precise force of the word in that sentence cannot be stated more narrowly.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “law.” It functions as a term identifying law within the Hebrew Old Testament. It occurs four times, all in four different verses, with references in Genesis and 1 Samuel. Its role is mainly relational to the surrounding wording, so the precise force in any particular verse depends on the sentence where it appears. The word’s recorded uses include passages associated with birth, death, and speech.

This Hebrew word means “merciful.” It describes showing mercy toward another person, expressing a response shaped by compassionate concern rather than harshness. The word appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Genesis 19:16 and Isaiah 63:9. Its use can identify mercy as the quality or action being expressed in a situation. The exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains a merciful response toward someone in need.

This Hebrew word means “haste,” describing hurried action or movement without delay. It functions as a noun for the condition or manner of acting quickly. The word occurs three times in the Old Testament, with each occurrence rendered “haste.” Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is clear: prompt, hurried action rather than slow or leisurely movement.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to fierce anger or wrath—an intense, forceful expression of displeasure. It commonly describes wrath directed against wrongdoing or rebellion, especially in passages speaking about God’s response to sin. The word occurs 41 times in the Old Testament, so it represents a recurring biblical description rather than a rare expression. Its role is usually that of the object of an action: wrath may be carried out, turned away, or provoked. The approved meaning term “fierce” highlights the word’s strength and severity.

This Hebrew word means “darkness,” referring to a condition in which light is absent or hidden. It appears five times in the Old Testament, in Genesis, Psalms, and Isaiah. Its normal function is to name darkness as a condition, while the surrounding passage determines its particular force in each verse. The central meaning remains darkness, whether the word describes an actual condition or is used within a passage’s contrast with light.

This Hebrew word means “right.” It functions as a directional word, identifying the right side or position rather than expressing an action or quality by itself. It occurs 33 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including repeated use in Leviticus and occurrences in Exodus, Kings, Chronicles, and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains the designation of what is right.

e.t: This Hebrew verb expresses going out, coming forth, or moving from one place or condition into another. It commonly describes people, things, or actions emerging, departing, or being brought out. In some sentences, the movement is outward; in others, the sense is that something or someone is brought forth. It is a very common Old Testament word, occurring 1,076 times, so its precise English rendering depends on the sentence. Its central idea remains movement outward or emergence from a source or location.

This Hebrew word refers to spit—the act or substance of spitting. It occurs three times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, in two verses: twice in Numbers 12:14 and once in Deuteronomy 25:9. In each setting, the word describes spitting as an outward physical act. Its use in these passages keeps the meaning concrete rather than presenting an abstract idea. The precise force of the act in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself means “spit.”

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “hostility”—active opposition or enmity between people or groups. It names a condition of strained conflict rather than an action by itself. In the Old Testament, it appears five times, describing persistent opposition in passages from Genesis, Numbers, and Ezekiel. Its use can refer to hostility between opposing parties and to hatred expressed against another. The surrounding verse determines who is involved and how that opposition is being expressed.

Jesharelah is a Hebrew personal name. It functions as a proper name, identifying an individual rather than expressing a general action, quality, or object. This name occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 25:14, and the English rendering preserves it as “Jesharelah.” Without the surrounding verse text, no further contextual significance should be assigned to the name itself.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “cup.” It names a cup as an object in a sentence and may refer to one used in ordinary service, royal settings, or temple vessels. Scripture also uses the word figuratively for what a person receives or experiences. It occurs 34 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Habakkuk. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word means “destruction.” It names the condition or result of being destroyed, serving as a term for destruction rather than identifying a person or describing an action. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Job 21:20. Because the word appears only there and the verse text is not included here, its exact force in that sentence belongs to the surrounding context.

e.t: This Hebrew word describes something as “flattering”—an expression or action shaped to please, honor, or win favor. Its uses include language directed toward people and wording connected with taking or assigning a name, so the surrounding sentence determines the precise force. The central idea remains conduct or speech that flatters. This Hebrew word describes speech marked by either “mockers” or “stammering.” It can point to derisive speech from people who ridicule others, or to halting, difficult-to-understand speech. The word occurs twice in the Old Testament, once in Psalm 35:16 and once in Isaiah 28:11. These uses show a connection with speech, while the surrounding passage determines whether the emphasis is mocking behavior or stammering expression.

“Lappidoth” is a personal name identifying an individual in the Hebrew Old Testament. It appears only once, in Judges 4:4, so its basic function is to identify a person rather than describe an action, quality, or object. The name is connected in the SEE record with the Hebrew entities for Israel and judge at that reference, but the available information does not provide enough verse text to explain the person’s specific role or significance there.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “garments” and refers to articles worn by a person. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, once in 2 Samuel 10:4 and once in 1 Chronicles 19:4. In both places, it names garments as a concrete object, functioning as the thing involved in the sentence rather than describing an action, person, or quality. Its basic sense is therefore straightforward: garments. It identifies what is worn.

e.t: Madmannah is a Hebrew proper name, referring to a place or settlement rather than expressing an action, quality, or ordinary object. It appears twice in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, in Joshua 15:31 and 1 Chronicles 2:49. The form is rendered “Madmannah,” so the name is preserved rather than translated into an English meaning. Its appearance in a genealogy also confirms its use as an identifying name within Israel’s recorded history.

e.t: This Hebrew verb means “endow,” expressing an action of granting or assigning something. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both occurrences within Exodus 22:16. Because the available wording is limited and no verse text is provided here, the word’s precise force in that passage depends on its surrounding context. Its role is verbal: it describes what someone does rather than naming a person, object, or quality.

This Hebrew word means “these,” pointing to particular people or things already identified in the surrounding statement. It functions as a demonstrative expression, directing attention to more than one item rather than naming or describing those items themselves. In the Hebrew Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both occurrences appearing in Ezra 5:15. Its exact reference depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic role is to identify a specific group or set as “these.”

This Hebrew word refers to possession—something held, owned, or belonging to someone. It appears three times in the Old Testament corpus, where its rendered sense concerns what a person or people possess. The word can describe possessions in a concrete sense, while its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage. Its uses occur in Job, Isaiah, and Obadiah, showing that it serves as a noun-like term for what is possessed rather than an action or command.

e.t: This Hebrew word expresses being “brought,” describing what happens to someone or something. It serves as the action word in its sentences, functioning as a predicate rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs three times, with “brought” appearing in two recorded renderings. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and sentence.

The Hebrew word refers to “furrows,” the long channels made in soil by plowing. It functions as a noun naming these visible lines or cuts in cultivated ground. This word occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing once in 1 Samuel and twice in Psalm 129. Its basic meaning remains concrete and agricultural: it identifies the marks made across the earth rather than an action or a person.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to a “refuge.” It names a place associated with protection and safety, rather than an action or a person. In the Old Testament, it occurs 20 times, chiefly in Numbers and Joshua, where refuges are spoken of as provisions that were given and established. The word also appears in Chronicles, showing that this idea remained part of Israel’s appointed places. Its central meaning is therefore a refuge: a location to which someone may turn for protection.

This Hebrew word means “respect,” naming the quality or attitude of showing respect toward someone. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 2 Chronicles 19:7, so its recorded use is limited to that single passage. In the sentence, it functions as the thing connected with the action or attitude being described. The surrounding verse determines exactly how this respect is expressed there.

This Hebrew word refers to “oppression”—the harsh or unjust treatment that presses people down. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Isaiah 5:7, so its ordinary meaning is represented by that single occurrence rather than by a broad range of passages. The word functions as a concise description of oppressive treatment; its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. Here, it is connected directly with the Lord’s dealings with his people.

Nebuchadnezzar is a personal name, not a general word describing an idea or action. It identifies the same person throughout its Hebrew Old Testament usage. The name appears 33 times, in Ezra and Daniel, with most occurrences in Daniel. English Bibles consistently render it as “Nebuchadnezzar,” so its ordinary meaning is the person’s name rather than a translatable quality or concept.

Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

The surrounding verse context determines what is being said about Ebronah in each occurrence.

Its repeated use presents help as a real source of support rather than merely an abstract idea. The precise emphasis in any verse depends on its surrounding context.

“Amasiah” is a personal name, identifying one individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 2 Chronicles 17:16.
